aries.text: Your fiery sign usually lights up the room, but today, a cozy corner with a loved one may be more your groove than pulling off the “life of the party” role. With the nurturing Cancer moon settling into your fourth house of home and family, you’re craving heart-to-hearts over hoopla. Of course, that quest for one-on-one time is easier said than done if there are guests milling about. Slip off for a walk or some cozy conversation in the quietest part of the house (doors closed). Just don’t hide away the entire time. An inspiring conversation about a creative project could set ambitious plans in motion before the dessert plates are cleared.

taurus.text: Repeat after us, Taurus: “I am thankful for (fill in the blank).” With the sentimental Cancer moon in your third house of communication, the words flow easily today, so put them to good use. Who are you spending the day with? Pick a few things to appreciate about each of them, then say them out loud (a toast between courses works nicely). Lift the spirits of your celebration by asking people what they’re most thankful for this year. The feel-good buzz will be palpable by the time the turkey is carved.

gemini.text: Today’s sky puts you in your dual-natured element: Half of you is fluttering about in social butterfly mode while the other half wants to settle down for a long winter’s nap. Credit the cozy Cancer moon in your second house of comfort and simple pleasures, which has you savoring every bite (and every couch cushion). Take people in small doses. An hour or two here and there will be more your speed than an all-night party. And if you decide to skip the whole turkey ordeal and decamp to a restaurant followed by a movie, consider it a perfectly valid tradition.

cancer.text: Put a couple extra chairs around the table, Cancer—two, not ten. With your ruler, the moon, in your sign today, you’re in your nurturing element and eager to share your bounty with everyone you love. Go ahead and lay it on thick, but pace yourself so you don’t burn out before the pie comes out. Your already invited guests deserve your full care and loving attention. That said, there are probably one or two beloved souls in your circle who don’t have plans for the day. Loop them into your celebrations like the extended family they are.

leo.text: Feeling a little more low-key than usual, Leo? With the dreamy Cancer moon drifting through your twelfth house of rest and reflection, you may prefer to let someone else hold court at the table today. Enjoy the break from performing! Since Mars just exited your sign yesterday after two months of nonstop motion, you’ve earned a breather. If an old memory or lingering hurt surfaces, slip off for a walk with a trusted friend and talk it through. Then come back for dessert. By the time nightlife beckons, you’ll be ready to hit the dance floor feeling lighter.

virgo.text: A traditional feast with all the trimmings? You could pull it off with your eyes closed, Virgo, but with the sociable Cancer moon in your eleventh house of friends and groups, it’s way more fun as a team effort. Call for backup so you’re not locked down in the kitchen all day. Turn it into a Friendsgiving potluck or delegate the sides while you give out-of-town guests the grand tour of your hometown’s latest haunts. Later, take a walk through the crisp air and peek in the shop windows for a preview of tomorrow’s Black Friday steals. Map out your plan of attack!

libra.text: You’re the glue who holds everyone together this turkey day, Libra, and with the nurturing Cancer moon in your tenth house of leadership, you may wind up running the show. Just don’t sacrifice self-care in the process, especially with Mars now in your restorative twelfth house. Do some damage control in advance by preparing a playlist of intergenerational jams and setting up a play area for the kids. A tray of signature cocktails can warm everyone up pre-meal. And if an elder at the table starts sharing a story you’ve never heard, pull up a chair and listen.

scorpio.text: Turkey day with a side of adventure? With the Cancer moon in your ninth house of travel and expansion, you might be celebrating far from home or with a new crew whose traditions differ from yours. Embrace the novelty and ask about the dishes on the table, since there’s often a great story behind a family recipe. Keep the good vibes flowing by openly acknowledging what you adore about everyone in your midst. Just don’t lose track of time (easy for live-for-the-moment Scorpios to do). Showing up late to the dinner table could bring unnecessary friction with your gracious host.

sagittarius.text: “’Tis better to give” could be your mantra today as the soulful Cancer moon in your eighth house leaves you awash in gratitude for the people who’ve truly shown up for you. Pay it forward by picking up a volunteer shift at a shelter or playing sous chef to whoever is preparing the seasonal feast. Later, steal a quiet moment with someone close and let them know exactly what they mean to you. That heart-to-heart will stay with you long after the leftovers are gone.

capricorn.text: Thanksgiving for two, anyone? With the affectionate Cancer moon lighting up your seventh house of partnerships, your closest one-on-one connections take center stage today. Single? A flirtatious attraction could heat up between courses and might even find you slipping out for a memorable kiss. Coupled? Although the demands of family and guests could activate your people-pleasing side, circle an hour for romantic “just the two of us” time. Bundle up and walk gloved hand in hand or take a drive to see a holiday light display (sexy roadside makeout session a plus).

aquarius.text: Your free-spirited sign isn’t usually one for sticking to a schedule, but today a little structure keeps the holiday humming. With the helpful Cancer moon in your sixth house of service and wellness, you’re happy to pitch in, whether that’s chopping veggies or running the dishwasher brigade. Just don’t over-function, Aquarius. Delegate a task or two so you’re not stuck in the kitchen while everyone else is having fun. Before the festivities begin, squeeze in a morning yoga class or a brisk walk to set a balanced tone for the day.

pisces.text: Will this be a three-hanky Thanksgiving for you, Pisces? With the tender Cancer moon in your fifth house of joy and self-expression, you’ll well up with gratitude for the ones you love (and maybe laugh until you cry, too). Don’t hold back your appreciation. Raise a toast to someone at the table who made a huge difference for you in 2026. If there are kids around, join the game of charades or lead a round of pie decorating. Your playful side is the life of this party!

items.title: Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
items.originalTitle: Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are now used by one billion people worldwide. What is their impact on human users?
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are now used by one billion people worldwide. What is their impact on human users? Popular narratives of concern argue that AI may be undermining our cognitive abilities, polluting our information ecosystem, corroding human relationships, damaging our mental health and rendering us vulnerable to persuasion, manipulation, emotional dependence and social engineering. Does the empirical evidence support these claims? Emerging research has begun to study the impact that AI has on people, via model evaluations, user studies, analysis of consumer chatlogs and agent-based simulations. Here we review this evidence, finding limited evidence for the strongest narratives of concern. However, research is still nascent and many uncertainties remain to be resolved in future work.

items.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Decline in Community-Dwelling Elders Who Die as Centenarians
items.originalTitle: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Decline in Community-Dwelling Elders Who Die as Centenarians
items.summary: Background and objectives: Brain pathologies are common in the elderly; however, their contribution to Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in those who die as centenarians remain unclear.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Background and objectives: Brain pathologies are common in the elderly; however, their contribution to Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in those who die as centenarians remain unclear. This study examines the frequency of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes (ADNC), limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC), and other brain pathologies and their association with Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in centenarians.

Methods: This clinicopathologic study included older participants from the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project, 2 ongoing clinicopathologic cohort studies of aging and dementia, who underwent annual clinical evaluations and autopsy. Participants were evaluated annually for cognitive status and followed for a mean (SD) of 11.4 (5.3) years before death. Neuropathologic evaluation included ADNC (and separately β-amyloid load and tangle density), LATE-NC, presence or absence of neocortical Lewy bodies (LBs), hippocampal sclerosis of aging (HS-A), primary age-related tauopathy (PART), and 5 cerebrovascular disease (CVD) pathologies including arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, macroinfarcts, and microinfarcts. Multivariable regression and linear mixed-effects models were applied.

Results: A total of 104 centenarians were included in this study. The mean (SD) age at death was 102 (1.9) years, 84% were female, 58% had Alzheimer dementia, 21% had mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 21% had no cognitive impairment (NCI). All 3 clinical diagnostic groups exhibited pathologies, including any type of CVD (94%), ADNC (72%; 73% of them were intermediate and 27% of them were high), LATE-NC (58%, 30% of them exhibiting HS-A), HS-A (18%, 95% had LATE-NC), PART (28%), and neocortical LBs (11%). Mixed pathologies, particularly ADNC + LATE-NC + CVD, were common in the Alzheimer dementia group (52%) compared with NCI (36%) and MCI (23%). After adjusted for age at death, sex, education, and other brain pathologies, only LATE-NC and tangles (specifically intermediate/high ADNC with Braak stage V) were associated with more rapid decline in global cognition and increased odds of Alzheimer dementia.

Discussion: Brain pathology, but not dementia, is nearly inevitable in those who die as centenarians. LATE-NC and tangles are the key contributors to cognitive decline. Future study investigating resilience factors may inform preventive strategies.

items.title: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain
items.originalTitle: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain
items.summary: Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience. Multilingual neural network models offer a way to answer this question by representing linguistic content across languages in a shared space. Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Here we combined existing (12 languages across 4 language families) and newly collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data (9 languages across 4 families) to test encoding models predicting brain activity in the language network using representations from multilingual models. Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. This cross-lingual generalization extended across variation in language family, stimulus type and presentation modality. These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.

items.title: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.originalTitle: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.summary: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm-2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm-2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. However, achieving high-performance wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) remains a significant challenge because of their high interface trap density (Dit) and large threshold voltage (VTH) variation. Here we show the distinct polarization switching mechanisms of AlScN FeFETs based on an ultrathin indium gallium oxide (IGO) channel with three different structures. FeFETs with a metal-ferroelectric-metal-insulator-semiconductor (MFMIS) structure show high interface quality with low Dit and a stable VTH, achieving a large memory window (MW) of up to 20.6 V and a high endurance of 106. The stable 6-bit operation of our devices with 64 distinct states shows the feasibility of multilevel storage applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the FeFET in neuromorphic networks, with a high recognition accuracy of 93.02%.

items.title: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit
items.originalTitle: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit
items.summary: Nitric oxide (NO) produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is a key regulator of animal physiology. Here, we uncover a function for NO in the integration of UV exposure and the gating of a UV-avoidance circuit.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is a key regulator of animal physiology. Here, we uncover a function for NO in the integration of UV exposure and the gating of a UV-avoidance circuit. We studied UV/violet avoidance mediated by brain ciliary photoreceptors (cPRCs) in larvae of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii. In the larva, NOS is expressed in interneurons (INNOS) postsynaptic to cPRCs. UV stimulation of cPRCs triggers INNOS activation and NO production. NO signals retrogradely to cPRCs to induce their sustained post-stimulus activation through an unconventional guanylate cyclase. This late activation drives ciliary beating through serotonergic ciliomotor neurons during UV avoidance. In NOS mutants, retrograde signalling, ciliary activation, and UV avoidance are defective. By mathematical modelling, we recapitulate phototransduction and circuit dynamics in wild-type and mutant larvae. Our results reveal how NO-mediated retrograde signalling gates a synaptic circuit and induces short-term memory of UV exposure to orchestrate light-avoidance behaviour.

items.title: Education-related polygenic scores show different associations with youth mental health in parent-offspring trios
items.originalTitle: Education-related polygenic scores show different associations with youth mental health in parent-offspring trios
items.summary: Educational attainment and mental health are associated from childhood, but less is known about how this association is reflected within families, where children's genetic variation is correlated with both parental genotypes and family environments.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Educational attainment and mental health are associated from childhood, but less is known about how this association is reflected within families, where children's genetic variation is correlated with both parental genotypes and family environments. We examine whether associations involving children's own and parental polygenic scores differ for cognitive and non-cognitive genetic components of educational attainment. These scores aggregate common DNA variants using weights from genome-wide association studies. We analyse 3,223 mother-father-child trios from the UK Millennium Cohort Study using structural equation models that jointly estimate associations involving children's own and parental polygenic scores. Here we show that cognitive and non-cognitive education-related polygenic scores are associated with externalising behaviour, including hyperactivity and conduct problems, and internalising behaviour, including anxiety and low mood, across childhood and adolescence. Associations are generally larger in magnitude for externalising than internalising behaviour, with clearer component-specific differences for externalising behaviour. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in education-related polygenic score associations with youth mental health within families.

items.title: Human brain organoids reveal MGE interneuron defects independent of mTOR-hyperactivation in genetic focal epilepsy
items.originalTitle: Human brain organoids reveal MGE interneuron defects independent of mTOR-hyperactivation in genetic focal epilepsy
items.summary: The pathogenic mechanisms of non-acquired focal epilepsy (NAFE) are underexplored. As the most common monogenic cause of NAFE, the epileptogenic mechanism of mutations in the GTPase-Activating Protein Activity Toward Rags 1 (GATOR1) genes remains unclear.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: The pathogenic mechanisms of non-acquired focal epilepsy (NAFE) are underexplored. As the most common monogenic cause of NAFE, the epileptogenic mechanism of mutations in the GTPase-Activating Protein Activity Toward Rags 1 (GATOR1) genes remains unclear. Here, using patient-derived neuron-type-specific organoids, we show that focal epilepsy-associated transcriptional dysregulation is highly pronounced in ventral GABAergic organoids (VGOs). Patient VGOs exhibit significant impairments in GABAergic interneuron differentiation, migration, and functional GABA release. Mechanistically, these interneuron defects are independent of the canonical mTOR-hyperactivation and are instead driven by the deficiency of MAFB. MAFB expression is significantly decreased in both patient-derived VGOs and brain tissues. MAFB knockdown leads to similar interneuron defects in VGOs. Importantly, MAFB overexpression rescues the abnormal phenotypes in patient VGOs. Collectively, our study reveals a non-canonical cellular and molecular mechanism underlying GATOR1-related focal epilepsy, providing a mechanistic basis for precise therapy.

items.title: Active locomotion predictively rescues head direction attractor dynamics in head-fixed mice
items.originalTitle: Active locomotion predictively rescues head direction attractor dynamics in head-fixed mice
items.summary: Head direction (HD) cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus form the brain's internal compass, and are often modeled as a ring attractor maintaining azimuth coding by leveraging continuous visual and inertial sensory input.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: Head direction (HD) cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus form the brain's internal compass, and are often modeled as a ring attractor maintaining azimuth coding by leveraging continuous visual and inertial sensory input. Here, we test how the common experimental preparation of head-fixed animals alters this code. Complete head-fixation that creates vestibular conflict disrupts both unit and population encoding of head direction, while selectively constraining head-on-body movements either in real or virtual reality uniquely impairs HD population activity. More specifically, attractor dynamics are altered in head-restrained male mice during periods of immobility, and a computational model recapitulates this effect by perturbing lateral connectivity among HD neurons. These dynamics recover several hundred milliseconds prior to locomotion onset, suggesting that an efference copy or prediction of a re-afferent signal is necessary to maintain HD network activity during head restraint. More generally, the results indicate that the HD network is a context- and state-dependent predictive estimator, stabilized by forthcoming self-motion signals. The classic ring-attractor models should be revised to integrate context-dependent dynamics with prospective motor signals, offering a more complete account of how the brain's compass remains stable across both naturalistic and constrained conditions.

items.title: The Sleep-Aging-Motor Memory Triad: A Systematic Review of Task-Dependent Consolidation and Neuroplasticity
items.originalTitle: The Sleep-Aging-Motor Memory Triad: A Systematic Review of Task-Dependent Consolidation and Neuroplasticity
items.summary: Motor learning includes a set of processes linked to practice and experience that are crucial for gaining new skills and altering behavior as time progresses. Proficiency in motor skills is crucial for maintaining autonomy and enhancing quality of life in older adults.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract: Motor learning includes a set of processes linked to practice and experience that are crucial for gaining new skills and altering behavior as time progresses. Proficiency in motor skills is crucial for maintaining autonomy and enhancing quality of life in older adults. Nonetheless, recent findings indicate that age-related sleep alterations significantly impair motor memory consolidation, thus speeding up the decline of motor abilities. Within this context, motor learning depends not only on internal neural processes but also on sleep quality, especially the preservation of slow-wave and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Disruptions to these sleep stages may interfere with the neural processes necessary for the long-term consolidation of motor skills. This synthesis emphasizes the importance of recognizing the relationship among sleep, aging, and sensorimotor plasticity, while suggesting effective intervention strategies like improving sleep or specific therapies to alleviate age-related motor deficits. These findings originate from a pre-registered systematic review of 26 research articles extracted from 740 sources indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. We investigated these effects on motor learning and whether they vary by task type, complexity, sleep effect, and age. This review seeks to enhance our comprehension of age-suitable empirical studies on sleep-related motor memory consolidation among healthy groups by synthesizing results from various research projects.

items.title: Unemployment, mental health and health promotion: a realist synthesis of international meta-analyses
items.originalTitle: Unemployment, mental health and health promotion: a realist synthesis of international meta-analyses
items.summary: Negative effects of unemployment on health have been known since the early stages of industrialisation. However, no adequate health-promoting strategy for coping has been identified to date. Research has developed in phases but remains heterogeneous and complex.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Negative effects of unemployment on health have been known since the early stages of industrialisation. However, no adequate health-promoting strategy for coping has been identified to date. Research has developed in phases but remains heterogeneous and complex. This realist synthesis examines the associations between unemployment and mental health and the mechanisms by which health promotion works, with a view to informing policy and practice.

Methods: A literature search was conducted in MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science and Health Evidence. The realist synthesis included ten systematic reviews with quantitative meta-analysis: seven on associations between unemployment and health and three on health promotion. The quality of the meta-analyses was assessed using the AMSTAR II checklist.

Results: Based on cross-sectional and longitudinal studies, the meta-analyses consistently show that mental health deteriorates significantly following job loss and improves after re-employment. Mental health impairment increases with the duration of unemployment. Moderator analyses indicate that unemployed men are more adversely affected than unemployed women. The evidence also shows that health promotion can produce both health and labour-market effects among unemployed people.

Conclusions: These meta-analyses support the hypothesis of a causal relationship between unemployment and health and have implications for research and health reporting. Health promotion measures can mitigate the downward spiral.
